items.question: Why did you choose to pursue a master’s at Columbia in the United States after accepting a PhD offer from the Chinese University of Hong Kong?
items.object: Choosing a Columbia master’s program after accepting a PhD offer from the Chinese University of Hong Kong
items.answer: It was indeed because many people were going abroad at the time. But I learned about the idea of going abroad rather late. I think moving from Jiangxi to university for my undergraduate degree gave me a strong sense of culture shock. The people around me understood career development and life development better; they had more plans. I was actually in a state of ignorance. When I first graduated from undergrad, I initially didn’t get into anything. I applied to U.S. universities, but at first I did not receive an offer. At the time I had an offer for a PhD from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, and I accepted it. I remember there was a gentleman’s agreement during applications. On April 15, the day after the gentleman’s-agreement deadline had already passed, I suddenly received a very ordinary graduate admission offer from Columbia—a master’s offer. It was really a very ordinary offer, one many people could get. But at the time I felt that I wanted to encounter something new, because the academic center was still in the United States. I wanted to go out and see it. Even though Columbia’s master’s program was not especially top-tier, I hoped to see it. I called my dad and asked whether we could renege on the earlier PhD offer. I would need to pay a penalty. But I wanted to go out and see. I hesitated, called my dad, and he said yes very quickly—within one minute: go. So I paid the penalty.

items.question: How do you think about what matters most when optimizing an SMT solver for formal verification?
items.object: SMT solver optimization in formal verification
items.answer: The field is broad, but I can briefly describe one part of what I worked on. One topic was to break down and map code written by humans, mapping it to underlying mathematical logic. You can map code to first-order logic. Once that logic is available, you can prove from a mathematical perspective whether the code you wrote has a certain property. More concretely, a piece of code has something called a specification. A spec states what preconditions the code should meet, what invariants it will have, and what conditions should be met after the code executes. You can use such a language to describe a program. What you prove is whether, given this spec, your code truly conforms to that logic. After mapping code to logical formulas, proving and reasoning among those formulas is the research field I worked in and what an SMT solver does. Most of my research was on optimizing the SMT solver itself. Optimization relates on one hand to efficiency and on the other to correctness, but more importantly to how you define semantics: what kind of semantic space you define to express what a piece of code does.

items.question: How do you view your early research success in formal methods at Stanford from the inside?
items.object: Early research success in formal methods at Stanford
items.answer: The real process was much drier, much more boring, than what the résumé looks like from the outside. My first few years at Stanford did not go smoothly. First, finding an advisor in my first year was not smooth. I entered formal methods somewhat passively. Because I had to complete my PhD, I had to keep doing research in this area and producing papers. I was in a relatively passive state. Of course, in the process I gradually came to appreciate its beauty. Later, I slowly understood why it was interesting, and developed more thoughts about it. I felt it also had an interesting future. But when I first worked on the Politeness paper—the one that first won IJCAR Best Paper—it was very, very unexpected. I was a complete beginner and knew nothing about the field. My advisor gave me a problem, and I simply solved it. When I finished it, I had no idea what counted as the best paper in the field, because I had not read enough papers. So when the award came out, I did not expect it at all; I learned I had won when others congratulated me. It was the first paper I published in the field. But after it, I returned to a very low state. I still had not found what the next problem I wanted to do was, or where an exciting problem was. After that paper, I remember the pandemic began. During the pandemic, I did nothing for as long as a year—close to a year—in a depressed state.

items.question: What made working on the proof in the Sequence paper so fulfilling for you?
items.object: The proof in the Sequence paper
items.answer: Only after a year, when I slowly emerged from it, did I write the Sequence paper. We had many struggles beforehand. The proof was probably more than twenty pages. We revised it four or five times, and twice I nearly threw out and rewrote the entire proof. A proof that had taken one or two weeks to derive, more than ten pages long, was completely discarded because we found an incorrect base point at the beginning. Once that was wrong, all subsequent reasoning was wrong. So the proof had to be corrected from the front, then entirely discarded and redone. But once we completed the process, it was very satisfying. When the proof was fully written, it was much more complicated than we had initially imagined. We all felt that writing that proof and having that experience was very accomplished, very fulfilling. I remember Clark himself said that the proof in that paper was his highlight of the past year. It was also nominated for Best Paper, though that was not public. It was discussed and ultimately not selected, but it came very close. If I had stayed in formal methods, that paper might have been the period I enjoyed most. Starting from that paper, I saw formal theory’s deeper meanings and beauty.

items.question: What do you find beautiful about the formal-methods perspective on programming-language design?
items.object: The formal-methods perspective on programming-language design
items.answer: It let me understand programming-language design from several different angles. The formal-methods approach designs languages by understanding programming languages mathematically. I had dealt with programming languages for a long time—twenty years—but I had never viewed them from that angle. It gave me an entirely new perspective. But you discover many trade-offs in programming languages. Some languages are closer to mathematics; some closer to hardware. It is hard to find a point where a language is close to both mathematics and hardware. Languages closer to mathematics are easier to verify and formalize. Languages closer to hardware are more flexible, more efficient, and closer to human habits of thought. When you need to program concrete operations in hardware, that mapping is more direct.

items.question: Why is building RadixArk as an infra-first company important to you?

items.question: How do you put infrastructure first when running training tasks at RadixArk?

items.question: How do you explain the core idea behind RadixAttention in SGLang?
items.object: RadixAttention’s reuse and management of shared-prefix KV caches
items.answer: It is actually fairly simple. When we have many requests sent to an engine for processing, if those requests have a common prefix, then we do not need to recompute the KV cache corresponding to that common prefix. We can reuse it. When the first request comes in, I have already computed the KV cache. When the second request comes in, if they share it, I can reuse the KV cache already computed. So this memory-management system indexes and stores the shared prefix structure. First, for the prefix relationships among incoming requests, we need to build a prefix tree for indexing. After indexing, we need to store the computed KV cache in a KV memory pool, then map that indexing to the KV memory pool.

items.question: How do you think increasingly powerful AI will change humanity’s future?

But that strength is functional strength: it will replace some human functions in terms of productivity. It cannot completely replace humans; it only replaces some human functions. items.question: What does LMSYS mean to you as a way to make research opportunities and recognition more equal?
items.object: LMSYS and equality in research recognition
items.answer: LMSYS came from when Lianmin and I initially wanted to create an institution where people from different schools could participate in research. To this day, although LMSYS is a nonprofit and we all help with things there part-time, it is something we want to do very seriously. If one day RadixArk—I hope it goes on forever—but if one day it does not go all the way, LMSYS is the cause I will pursue for my entire life. It has something in common with RadixArk: they share values concerning equality and equal rights. LMSYS’s equal rights come from our hope to incubate projects made by outstanding people even when they do not have sufficient background, backing, or brand. This also comes from some of my personal experiences. I have gone through very low periods and very high periods, and I can sense the difference. It may be the same me doing the same thing. During a high period, something I do is very easily noticed, remembered, and even exaggerated by others. But things I did during low periods were sometimes good too, yet it was hard for people to see or recognize them. I do not think that difference needs to exist, and it damages the structure of fair competition in society. What LMSYS hopes to do is flatten that difference: to help genuinely good projects be lifted up, and to ensure credit goes to the people doing the work, giving people who may not yet have accumulated or established a reputation stronger control over their projects. items.question: How do you understand the subtle gender asymmetries in how people recognize achievement?
items.object: Subtle gender asymmetries in how achievement is perceived
items.answer: It cannot really be called discrimination; it is not that serious. Call it gender inequality. It may not even rise to the level of inequality or discrimination, but there are many subtle asymmetries at the level of consciousness everywhere. Let me give you a subtle example—so subtle that you would feel it is not even an issue. As a child, I came from competitive programming and did very well in competitions. If I were a boy, people would say I was a genius. If I were a girl, they would say, “She works very hard,” “She is very obedient,” “You are very diligent.” Or, “You are lucky.” What I experienced as a child was this: in one year of competitions, my results had consistently been very good; in all kinds of major competitions, I was at the very top—at least much better than people my age at my school. But people around me would find countless reasons to explain why I was good. They thought it was not proper that I won. They did not deny that I was a genius—they would not deny it—but they felt that if someone else won, it was only natural. But if I won, they felt that my victory needed explaining. Under normal circumstances, a person’s victory does not need to be explained. Why should I explain why he won? He is capable.

But in the end, the investors and partners who truly matched us returned to the kind of relationship between investors and founders that I had seen in textbooks. The books had not deceived us.

Likewise, before my PhD, many people’s descriptions to me of the relationship between PhD advisors and students may have been overly beautiful. But in the end, I got those beautiful things. Those descriptions had not deceived me. There really are such pure, such good advisors in the world; such good investors; such good interviewers.

But most people do not persist through the whole up-and-down process. They do not persist in believing that those good things really exist. It is just that you have to filter; you have to be patient and wait for them to finally reveal themselves. You need the patience to let the grains of sand that are not the ideal state fall away on their own. Many people may start doubting in the middle, and then give up.

items.question: How do you reconcile your firmly held values with a world where things you believe should not happen keep happening?
items.object: Maintaining personal values when reality contradicts them
items.answer: Within my own logic, it is internally consistent. My logic is not disturbed by the things I see. There is pain, too—I do feel pain. I am actually a very emotional person. Many very small things can have a very large emotional impact on me. But I can separate that emotional impact from the construction of my values. For example, I see many things that I do not want to see; I do not want them to happen, but they all happen. Then I feel very unhappy. But after seeing them, it does not make me think that they are normal. I will still firmly believe that the things I have not seen but believe in are right. I will still firmly believe that there is a world I want to see, but I have not seen it yet. It is only that I have not seen it yet. I may believe in this for years, for ten years; I still believe it is there. This is difficult to change. But my past experiences have told me that these things do exist. In the end, I encountered all of them. So I have had a lot of positive feedback. But I think many people have not seen positive feedback, so you cannot ask everyone to persist. But I think I am lucky, because I have seen all the positive feedback. That positive-feedback cycle lets me persist for longer and longer when I encounter similar situations later. Maybe the first time, I waited several months, and it was validated. The next time, I waited several years, and it was validated. The time after that, I waited ten years, and it was validated again. But then I knew that it could always be validated. Next time I can wait twenty years; the time after that I can wait—well, perhaps by then life will be over. But I think, at least I waited for it; I think other people can wait for it too.

items.question: How do you think about staying true to your own convictions when they remain at odds with the world?
items.object: Remaining true to one's convictions when they conflict with the world
items.answer: You need to find that internal consistency. For example, say I waited ten years and finally got it, but some of my own understanding has always been misaligned with the world. During those ten years, I have always existed in a very split state. I think that is okay, too. I can also continue to exist in that split state. Even if my whole life is split, I do not want to compromise. Being able to find that boundary is important. Actually, having that split is completely okay. It will not truly be very painful. People are merely afraid. But if someone tells you, “That’s just how it is. It’s okay,” then it really is okay. But first of all, there is no absolute rightness in this world. I cannot say that I am a correct person. Everyone is a correct person. But I am only saying that everyone has their own ideas. What you consider correct may be incorrect in other people’s eyes, and that is okay—completely okay. There is no problem at all. The only key point is whether you understand and act according to your own ideas, or whether you are actually being led along by other people, or feel that you are compromising. As long as you do not feel that you are compromising, it is okay. Even if you are really wrong, then so be it; it is okay. But what I really dislike is everyone becoming unable to carry out their own will. That is not good. If everyone carries out their own will, then even if you are not harmonious, that too exists naturally; it is inherently valid.
